newsitem.title: UK: British markets hope for election victory.
newsitem.headline: British markets hope for election victory.

text.p: British financial markets would take a widely-expected election victory by the opposition Labour party next year in their stride, but an inconclusive result would trigger a steep slide across all fronts, analysts say.
A Reuters survey showed that UK shares, the pound and government bonds would show only a knee-jerk dip if Tony Blair's revamped party wins an overall majority of the next Parliament.
But fears are growing that neither Labour nor the ruling Conservatives will capture half of the 659 seats required for a decisive victory, producing a hung Parliament.
"What the markets are looking for is a clear result and a clear mandate," Steve Hannah, chief economist at IBJ International said.

"A hung parliament is the worst possible scenario because of the policy confusion which would arise...the lack of clarity and ...prospect of fresh elections within the year would be quite damaging," he said.

The mean of forecasts from 11 banks and financial institutions predicted the FTSE index of 100 leading shares would slide to 3745 points from an expected 3,855 just before a May general election. The index hit a record high of 4014.4 on Wednesday.
If Labour -- traditionally seen as a harbinger of inflation and rising interest rates -- win the election, the index will dip by a mere 20 basis points, the survey showed.

A fifth term in office for the ruling Conservatives would immediately send the FTSE much higher, but this is seen as the least likely outcome. Labour has kept a steady lead of between 20 and 30 basis points in recent opinion polls.

Economists said Labour's declared shift from policies of "tax and spend", coupled with a more friendly approach towards European economic and monetary union (EMU) had calmed market fears of a socialist government.
"I think we are well away from the world in which the idea of a Labour government creates mass panic in the City," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at Bank of America.
But economists note that continued uncertainty over many of Labour's actual policies once Blair has taken office would keep markets wary initially.

"Markets will take fright ahead of the election and we should see a sell-off," said Philip Shaw, economist at Union Discount. "With a Labour majority we see uncertainty continuing until they have proved their credentials."
Sixteen out of the 26 economists polled between September 24 and 26 believe Prime Minister John Major will wait until the May 1997 election deadline before going to the country.
The pound, expected to decline to 2.3185 marks ahead of that date from around 2.3905 earlier this week, should rally provided one of the two main parties wins a clear majority.
But an inconclusive vote would see the pound crashing to 2.2859 marks, the poll showed.

Most economists are confident official interest rates will be held steady at 5.75 percent before the election, but will have to rise by at least 25 basis points shortly afterwards regardless of which party wins.

The survey predicted the yield on ten-year gilts (government bonds) would rise to around 8.15 percent in the weeks before an election, as mounting inflation worries and fears of the consequences of opting out of EMU pushes prices down. This compares with a yield of less than 7.50 percent on Wednesday.
A Labour victory would have little effect, but a hung Parliament would push gilt yields slightly higher.

The yield spread between ten-year gilts and the comparable German Bund is also expected to widen to 184 basis points before the election from around 160 basis points now. It will widen to 191 basis points if the outcome was inconclusive, the poll said.
